title: Innovative Thermal Technologies — Ohmic, Dielectric, Infrared and Induction Heating
shortDescription: Electrical, electromagnetic and radiant heating methods and where each fits.
genZNote: Why heat food slowly from outside when you can make it heat itself from inside? Ohmic, RF, IR, induction — same goal, different electricity mood.

sections.heading: Comparison
sections.body: Compared to conventional heating, these methods shorten process time, reduce thermal damage and improve energy efficiency, but need capital, process control and validation for food safety.

table.caption: Heating technologies
rows: Electric current passes directly through food (Joule heating); depends on electrical conductivity
Pumpable foods with particles, juices, eggs, purees; aseptic processing
Rapid, uniform; electrodes and conductivity matter; no hot surfaces
Dipole rotation and ion conduction in an alternating electromagnetic field; RF at 13.56/27.12 MHz
Volumetric; RF penetrates deeper than microwaves
Radiant energy absorbed at the surface (wavelengths ~0.76–1000 µm)
Baking, roasting, drying, blanching, surface pasteurisation
Alternating magnetic field induces eddy currents in a metallic vessel or package
Cooking vessels, retort/aseptic heating, can sealing, thermal processing of liquids

sections.heading: Exam Notes
bullets: Ohmic: food acts as a resistor — higher salt content increases conductivity.
Dielectric loss factor determines heating rate; moisture and salt influence it.
Infrared heating is mostly a surface effect; microwave and RF are volumetric.
Induction heating requires a ferromagnetic/conductive material.
These are called innovative thermal technologies because heat is generated in situ rather than transferred slowly by conduction/convection.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Ohmic, dielectric, infrared and induction heating generate heat directly in or near the food using electricity, enabling fast and efficient thermal processing.

commonTraps: Do not say infrared penetrates deeply.

questions.prompt: Which method heats mainly the surface?
